source.title: Man's Search for Meaning
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of Man's Search for Meaning by Viktor E. Frankl (1946). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: When circumstances are taken from you, your response remains your own
cards.body:
Frankl, a psychiatrist, survived several Nazi concentration camps, where he lost most of his family. He observed that even when nearly everything was taken from prisoners, some still chose how to respond: sharing food, offering comfort or holding on to their dignity.

He concluded that a person keeps one inner freedom: the choice of attitude towards what happens. This is not a claim that suffering is fine, or that people who broke under it failed. It is a reminder that some choice usually remains, even in hard times.
cards.apply_it: When something outside your control goes wrong today, pause and ask: what response would I be proud of here?

quiz.question: What freedom did Frankl believe remains even in the worst conditions?
options: Freedom to leave
Freedom to choose one's attitude and response
Freedom from all suffering
Freedom to control others
quiz.explanation: He held that the choice of how to meet circumstances can't be fully taken away.

cards.title: A reason to keep going makes hardship easier to bear
cards.body:
Frankl noticed that fellow prisoners who had something to live for, such as a loved one to see again or work still to finish, seemed better able to endure. Those who lost all sense of a future often lost the will to continue. He borrowed an idea from Nietzsche: a person with a strong enough why can face almost any how.

Today, the lesson applies on a smaller scale. Hard stretches at work, study or recovery feel more bearable when connected to a purpose that matters to you.
cards.apply_it: Write down one hard thing you're doing right now and, next to it, the reason it matters to you. Keep it where you'll see it.

quiz.question: What did Frankl observe helped prisoners endure?
options: Physical strength alone
Avoiding all thoughts of the future
Luck only
Having a purpose or someone to live for
quiz.explanation: A sense of purpose and a future to work towards helped people hold on.

cards.title: Meaning can come from what you do, who you love and how you face suffering
cards.body:
Frankl founded logotherapy, an approach built on the idea that the main human drive is to find meaning. He suggested three broad routes to it: creating something or doing a deed, experiencing something or someone, especially through love, and the stance you take towards suffering you cannot avoid.

The third route doesn't mean seeking pain. When suffering can be prevented, it should be. But when it can't, how a person bears it can itself carry meaning.
cards.apply_it: Note one thing in each area this week: something you made or did, someone you appreciated, and a difficulty you faced with courage.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of Frankl's routes to meaning?
options: Doing a deed or creating a work
Loving someone or experiencing something deeply
Seeking out suffering on purpose
The attitude taken towards unavoidable suffering
quiz.explanation: Frankl said avoidable suffering should be avoided; meaning comes from how we bear what can't be changed.

cards.title: Instead of asking what life owes you, ask what it's asking of you
cards.body:
Frankl proposed flipping a familiar question. Rather than asking 'what is the meaning of life?' in the abstract, he suggested that life puts questions to each of us, through specific situations, people and tasks, and we answer by how we act.

This makes meaning concrete and personal. It isn't one grand answer you find once. It is found in responding responsibly to what is in front of you today, which differs from person to person and moment to moment.
cards.apply_it: At the start of tomorrow, ask: what is today asking of me? Pick one task or person and give it your full attention.

quiz.question: How did Frankl reframe the question of life's meaning?
options: Life owes us happiness
Meaning is the same for everyone
Life asks questions of us, and we answer through our actions
Meaning can only be found in books
quiz.explanation: He saw meaning as found in responding responsibly to specific situations.

cards.title: Happiness tends to follow from meaning rather than being chased directly
cards.body:
Frankl warned that aiming straight at happiness or success often backfires. The harder you chase them as goals in themselves, the more they can slip away. Instead, he saw them as side effects that arrive when you commit to something beyond yourself: a cause, a piece of work or another person.

He also described an 'existential vacuum', a sense of emptiness and boredom many people feel when life lacks direction, which people may try to fill with distraction rather than purpose.
cards.apply_it: Instead of asking 'what will make me happy?', ask 'what or who could I give myself to this week?' Do one thing towards it.

quiz.question: According to Frankl, how is happiness best reached?
options: As a by-product of dedicating yourself to something meaningful
By pursuing it directly and constantly
Through distraction
By avoiding responsibility
quiz.explanation: He believed happiness ensues from commitment to meaning rather than direct pursuit.
